It is an important issue as to the timeliness of an objection, and secondly, as to whether or not there is any requirement in the Rule that every single page of the full statement ought to be signed. It is the Prosecution submission, that, no, there is no such requirement. The question is whether or not they are entitled to cross-examine the expert, which they did. So, practically and simply, no, the answer is no, we do not necessarily need to rely on it but they are greatly matters of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your position. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, indeed this is not a question that would necessitate any further waste of time. We wish to know what these annexes covers but whether that Mr. Zecevic can be accepted as an expert witness since he was sent by the -- by Sarajevo, not by the Tribunal. Secondly, we raise this -- that is true somewhat late but after the fact because the Defence, if we have to present a document, an expert document, this document of the expert should have proper signatures. And according to what the Defence knows, as far as the Defence is aware, additional information on sheets of paper which is not signed has never been admitted in the international practice, or even outside it, as a kind of expert analysis. Therefore, since the Defence received all of these documents, we think that it should be rejected in its integral form, and not only the factor the text needs -- that certain parts need to be redacted from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Redacted. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand what you mean. Then another issue still pending was the 92 bis. May I first ask the Defence. I invited the Defence to clarify to the Chamber whether there were any new aspects, since the 92 bis statements have been filed for the second time, whether the -- I did understand from your last response, Ms. Pilipovic, that the response given at an earlier date that Defence would still consider this as the response to the 92 bis statements since they are the same, not all, but essentially they are the same as filed at that time. Are there any additional issues?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In point of fact you have interpreted but I would like to repeat, the Defence acted in line with 92 bis (E) because -- to the submission of the Prosecutor when he suggested on the 29th of January, 2002, and he suggested that some evidence, some proof of facts be made in accordance with Rule 92 bis and that we should supply our answer on the 5th of February of 2002. We believe that the motion by the Prosecution of the 6th of June, 2002, when the Defence was given the same material as was enclosed to the statements as regarded documentation and the statements, except that our learned friends in the Prosecution informed the Defence that they were withdrawing the two statements they intended to tender earlier in accordance with Rule 92 bis. We merely wish to point out that the documentation which was supplied annexed to these statements of the witness which the Prosecution wishes to tender in line with Rule 92 bis, is of the same quality as before, which means that the documentation is illegible and that therefore it cannot be put to proper use. The Defence has informed the Prosecution that the documentation is not legible but, however, we have not received an answer so far. So the Defence stands by its motions of the -- its motion of the 5th of February, 2002, and wishes to point out that when it come to so-called authenticity witnesses, as the Prosecution qualified some witnesses on the 20th of April in its submission of the 20th of June -- 24th of June 2002, the Defence, in line with 92 bis, says that the purpose of 92 bis is that the Prosecution wants to use Rule 92 bis in order to tender certain documentation which is not envisaged by 92 bis. Therefore, the Defence objects to the tendering of witness statements, and these are witnesses who are indicated in item 28 of the Prosecution submission on the 24th of June. The Defence can quote them, but because of the problems with their surnames, I therefore refer you to item 28. In other words, these are witnesses through which not only different documents are being tendered such as medical documentation, death certificates, maps, and a list of documents of the BH army which the Defence cannot accept because, in this manner, documents would be tendered which -- the source of which the Defence does not know and, therefore, doesn't know whether they are authentic or not. We also object to the tendering of death certificates through Rule 92 bis because such certificate are not a document proving that a person has died, and even less so, what were the causes of death, that is, the cause of death. As regards the statement of Adem Omerkic, a major in the BH army, the Defence points out that it has had no opportunity to see the original documents of the BH army which are in the list alongside the -- alongside Mr. Omerkic's statement. So that our final view as regards the authenticity of a certain number of documents which are on the list accompanying Mr. Omerkic's statement, we cannot present at this moment. The allegations of the Prosecution in their submission on the 24th of June, under 28, that these witnesses are not giving the statement or the authenticity, and the contents of these documents are unacceptable to the Defence because the documents which the Prosecution seeks to tender are documents whose authenticity the Prosecution wishes to confirm through the testimony of these witnesses. However, these witnesses cannot confirm the authenticity of these documents. The Defence points out that the context and the veracity of a document needs to be established through direct examination before the courts if the parties disagree. The Defence also wishes to point out that the Defence agrees that if written statements are produced under 92 bis, that we would also submit it into the Court and that, therefore, it is necessary to allow the Defence or rather the accused to cross-examine those witnesses whose statements have been tendered. And the right to cross-examination would be the only thing that would ensure a fair trial, which may not be neglected in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I just interrupt you. You know that Rule 92 bis says that the Chamber has to decide whether it admits a written statement and whether the witness should be called to -- for cross-examination. What you are telling us now is that if there is no cross-examination, that the trial would not be fair. That means that you say that Rule 92 bis is such that it opens for the Chamber the opportunity to decide, to choose, for an unfair trial. Should it not be of more assistance to the Chamber if you would indicate under what circumstances the Chamber might allow or might admit the statement without cross-examination of the witness and where cross-examination of the witness would be -- would be necessary, because what you are telling us now is that we should not apply Rule 92 bis. And of course, we will consider, if that is your point of view, whether we should or should not do so. It is not of great assistance, I think, if you do not give us any view on what, in the eyes of the Defence, should be the criteria. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, when it comes to the tendering of witness statements, wishing to confirm the authenticity of the documentation, I already said that these are witnesses indicated under item 28. To begin with, the Defence has no proof of the source of documents, that is, we have no evidence as to how those witnesses came by those documents, nor do we have the source of these documents, and that is one of the reasons for which the Defence wishes to cross-examine those witnesses. Secondly, I have already pointed out that when it comes to the documentation, the Defence has never seen the original documentation. Likewise, and thirdly, the third reason why it is necessary to hear the witnesses before the Court is the fact that so far the Defence has pointed out that some documents had been tampered with, as one can see from the photocopies. This goes especially for the documentation which was disclosed regarding the incident at Markale. When I speak -- when I say this, I mean the medical documentation, and that is one of the reasons why the Defence challenges the authenticity of each one of these documents. And in our submission for the 5th of February, we have already indicated by Professor Dinko Radnic needed to be heard. The same goes for Mr. Gavro Kapetanovic, therefore, all those witnesses whose statements the Prosecution seeks to tender and also, through the statements, to also tender the documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one additional question: Am I right, is my recollection right that in your earlier submission that you did not oppose against the statement of Kablar and I think also not of Omerkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have before me this submission as for the statements of witness Sefketa Krestalica and witness Dijana Kablar. Have pointed out the submission -- the Defence does not object to these two, and we could not get the third, Haveric. We do not object to their ... Of course, if these documents have not been forged, but we can establish it in the course of the proceedings. So in the submission of the 5th of February, these are the three statements where we pointed out that we did not object to the production of these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that is still the same because you are, in general terms, objecting against all authentication statements, and Kablar is among them. So that is the reason why I am just asking you specifically. I think Kablar authenticates three documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. As for the Defence submission of the 5th of February, in it the Defence has also analyzed in detail why is it necessary to examine the witness testifying about incidents which allegedly happened, and this has to do with alleged sniping and shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. But, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the 5th of February, we likewise explained in detail the reasons why is it necessary to examine the witnesses who, as the Prosecution alleges, who are witnesses who would be testifying about -- witnesses we have also explained in detail why they need to be cross-examined. The Defence is also under obligation -- the Defence is also under obligation to respond to the Prosecution's request to admit the statement of the late Hamdija Cavcic. The Defence considers that regardless of Rule 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to make -- to separate 92 bis (C) issues at this very moment. So let's first now look at the statements of witnesses that are not deceased.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in a motion on the 5th of February, we dealt in some detail with the statements of Witness N, whose statement the Prosecution seeks to tender. We pointed out that Witness N talks about the separation lines in her statements from the direction of incoming fire. And for the purposes of establishing these facts, the Defence deems it necessary for the witness -- for Witness N to be heard in court. As for Alisa Deljkovic, Kenan Jamakovic, these witnesses are also scheduled -- are also expected to testify on incidents, and for the purposes of verifying the relevant facts in the relevant times, the facts with which General Galic has been accused, it is necessary for them to be subjected to cross-examination, and also for the purposes of establishing their reliability and credibility. Your Honour, I can address these witnesses individually, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. If you are saying that you stick to your earlier submissions in this respect. Of course, we have read them and it is not -- there is no need to repeat them in court. But if there is anything additional to that, then we would like to hear that. And perhaps you could also respond to a submission made by the Prosecution which says that if, may I call them "sniping incidents," witnesses would have to be called because of the need to cross-examine them on the source of fire, that the Prosecution would alternatively seek the statements to be admitted, but without the parts concerning the -- concerning the source of fire. That would mean that they would mainly corroborate the incident as such that persons were injured or killed, but without the source of fire, that part of the statement to be admitted. Could you please respond to that as well? I did understand you well, Mr. Ierace, that it is the position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence cannot accept that only this portion of the statement be subject to the examination of the witness. These witnesses are talking of the wide area of Sarajevo. They were eyewitnesses to the events which took place there. And in order to verify the accuracy of the facts that they mention in their depositions, in their statements, the Defence believes that it is necessary to cross-examine them regarding the issues brought up in their statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is a clear position. Then, in your earlier submission, you said that the fact that someone of the Prosecutor's office was present during the -- during the procedure would make it impossible for the Defence to accept, since they were not invited, to admit these statements into evidence. Is that position still the Defence position?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then please explain to me how you interpret the practice directions which I would say prescribe the presence of the parties seeking the statement to be admitted during this procedure, I would say this verification procedure, more or less after the statement has been given the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have pointed out to the problem of the presence of the investigator who took the statement from the witness, when that statement was verified by the presiding officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the Rules of Procedure and Evidence - and I believe I have studied them quite carefully - do not provide for the presence of the investigator during the procedure of the verification of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the -- I think the practice directions do, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not "statement" but "declaration."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to practice direction on 92 bis. I have got the French text in front of me at this moment, under 6. I will read it in French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have the English translation of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I might not have it in front of me, as a matter of fact. Do we have the English text available for the interpretation? Yes, if I just try to read it -- it is only part of a line. It is about the officer who deals with it. It says: [Interpretation] "He shall request in particular the presence of a representative of the requesting party." [In English] So my question still is: Does the Defence take the position that this is an envelope procedure or -- I have some difficulties in understanding you, to complain about the presence of the representative of the requesting party and not spend one word on the directive that prescribes this procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence happens to know that the individual in question actually took the statement, was the same person who had initially taken the statement, but the Rule says that that should be a representative of the requesting party. That is the party that had taken the statement. I am referring specifically to the presence of Mr. Barry Hogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the representative of the requesting party isn't the requesting party, the Prosecution. We have two possibilities, I would say: Either the Defence or the Prosecution is the requesting party.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I fully understand that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Barry Hogan is the person who conducted interview. We don't know for sure whether he is acting in his capacity as a representative of the requesting party. I understand that he is an investigator who took the statement, and we actually object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now you say since it is Mr. Hogan -- so that is a totally different argument. Your argument was that no one should have been present when the Defence is not invited to be present. And now I do understand that you changed your position and you say Mr. Hogan is not qualified to act as a representative of the Prosecution during this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Actually, the Defence does not know whether he was that person in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that is clear to me now. Yes, one more question. You just told us that a death certificate is not a document to prove that someone is dead. Could you please explain to me what death certificate? I mean, I am not talking about the cause of death, but just about the death. What is a death certificate meant for, if not to prove that someone is dead or someone died?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that certificate and the so-called certificate on death are two different documents. Certificate on a person's death is issued by a hospital, whereas the regular death certificate is issued by the relevant authorities and it is designed to prove that a person has died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the hospital certificate is not, is not to prove that someone died?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, officially and formally speaking, certificate on the person's death is issued by the institution where the person in question died. And it was in that sense that I distinguish it from the death certificate. Once the certificate on death is forwarded to the relevant authorities, it is the relevant authorities who issue a formal death certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be the relevant authority on this in the same area where the hospital is. It is -- the title of the document is Excerpt from the Register -- from the book of deaths. The problem we had was the diagnosis which was written on these certificates. We saw this in the case of Markale. We saw that this information was stricken from these documents and that what we received were actually copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand your point. Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honour, my colleague wishes to add just a few words on this subject, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Generally speaking, one of the reasons why the Defence categorically opposes this is a principle. The admission of documents on the basis of Rule 92 bis is as follows: It is the examination of the witness Richard Mole that has provided us with this type of response. We saw that this witness -- in the case of this witness, it was during the cross-examination the witness made clear certain things which did not result from witness's previous statements, things which are obviously very important for establishing the truth. I am referring to the issue of hospitals and the questions that were asked by the Chamber. We base ourselves on the following principles: In respect of each of this statement and declaration, we have to be given the possibility to bring up other aspects of the case before the Chamber. This was evident today from the examination of this witness. It is not something that is important only for the Defence, it is also important for the Tribunal in general and it is in the interest of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand your position. May I -- may I ask whether the Prosecution has -- no, I'll perhaps, first ask Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I checked in the transcript of the statement of Professor Zecevic that he clearly indicated that the two interviews, that he recognised them, and that these were his statements given to the -- let me just read it to you. The question was: "Do you also see records of what you said in interviews that you gave to OTP officials on the 22nd of November, 2001, the 1st of March, 2002, in both English and B/C/S language?" "Yes." And then, "To the best of your knowledge and belief, Professor, is the information contained in all five of these documents true and accurate? " Then he said, with some perhaps mistakes in translation, but basically everything is there. So he clearly identified these two documents as reflecting the interviews he gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, do you wish me to state our position on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that if you say a document has not been signed, that there could be doubts as to the -- whether this document would reflect at least what the content of the document reflects. And by saying that these documents are true and accurate statements of what he declared, I mean, what's the -- is the signature better or necessary if there is an oral statement which clearly indicates what you would usually establish by looking at the signature under a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the objection is a two-fold one. First of all, there is a principle involved in this issue. When the Prosecution gives us, not a statement as such but only additional or supplementary information, we do not expect this to be treated as a statement which are part of a testimony. In this respect, I think that our rights are being infringed. The other aspect is a practical one. In cases of -- we have often seen contradictions being made as a result of translation or interpretation. So it is always possible there have been technical problems, translation problems, and so on and so forth, when the document is not confirmed by a signature. A signature confirms the integrity and accuracy of the document. So if the witness has not seen the statement, if he was not given the opportunity to read the statement, on having read it out, then we can cannot treat it in the same way. This almost amounts then to an expert statement and not merely a statement as a deposition, as a declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It falls within the field of the expertise of Professor Zecevic. May I ask the Prosecution to respond briefly on specifically the 92 bis statement which is followed by a long list of BiH documents of which the -- well, it's just a list at this moment. I remember that we discussed before whether we would like to be provided with all the documents, I think. Could the -- could the Prosecution -- I think it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the assistance of the usher, please, so that we can give this document to the Defence -- to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is Adem Omerkic. We are provided with a very, very, very long list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, we are just obtaining that statement now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What are we expected to do with this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you allow me a minute or so to confer with my colleagues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the Prosecution confirms -- confers, since this list has not been written in Esperanto, but almost, can the Prosecution tell us what the source of the document is and how it was written? It is partly in English and partly in Serbian. I really have, personally, problems reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that time, Mr. President. Mr. President, the statement has attached to it a number of documents which have come from the archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have talked about that previously. The document that is the statement was initially composed with various purposes in mind in terms of those annexures. The -- that time was previous -- was before we eliminated a number of witnesses from the witness list. There may or may not be some use made of some of the documents which are still annexed to the statement. Therefore, I propose that if it is convenient to the Trial Chamber, perhaps a decision could be made at this stage, along with the other 92 bis statements, as to whether it is within the confines of the Rule, and then at the end of the Prosecution case, we could assist the Trial Chamber by indicating specifically which documents we require to be tendered. I say that because there are some witnesses still to be called who may or may not use those documents. So rather than burden the Trial Chamber with a lot of additional paper at this stage, perhaps if that decision in principle could be made, then on the last few days we can hand up a list of those particular exhibits of which we, in fact, need. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have another question in respect of -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this new issue, the Defence opposes this way of proceeding. When exhibits are contaminated, you are first of all asked to give a theoretical decision, but we don't know what kind of exhibits will follow. The decision has to be a very specific one and concern specific documents and not be abstract in nature. We know now that we are dealing with the application of Rule 92 bis, but the decision should concern specific exhibits in terms of the application of 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand the position. The Chamber does understand the position of the Defence in this respect. Mr. Ierace, a question about a 92 bis statements of Salko Zametica. Do I understand that the Prosecution seeks to introduce, in one way or the other, the death certificate of, and is that attached to the statement? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is, Mr. President. And that is the only significance of his 92 bis statement. Indeed, there has already been evidence given by the deceased's daughter and the neighbour that she was shot twice, and in the case of the daughter at least, that her mother died. So it is corroborative in nature, and I don't recollect there being any suggestion in cross-examination that she did not die as a result of those wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic. You are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, concerning the issue of the admission of certificate on death for Salko Zametica, we have already explained why we wish to cross-examine Mr. Zametica regarding the incident in question. I merely wish to point out that the fact that a certificate on death is an official document and it can serve as proof that the person died but it does not explain the cause of death. Let me just remind you of the fact that such a fact needs to be proved with a post-mortem report, when a pathologist, a forensic expert, establishes the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I have the facts clearly in my mind, the evidence of the wife of Salko Zametica when trying to get water from the Dobrinja river with some shelter of a bridge, but giving up that shelter in order to get water out of the river, that she was hit -- it is not my recollection whether these are one or two bullets - I am not quite sure about that - but that on the spot the -- those who witnessed that event had to pull her out and that the evidence was that she was, as the persons around her saw, no sign of life any more. That is what my -- is it the position of the Defence that she died from any other cause than being hit by that bullet or bullets?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I just add to that - this may also jog your memory and that of the Defence - that there was much animated debate about the time of her death as a result of some hospital documentation that went into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we did not admit all the medical records. We did not admit one, as far as my recollection goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, but I should say in relation to the time of death, not whether it was a different day but whether it was 1.00 or 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it is the position of the Defence, Ms. Pilipovic, that the wife of Salko Zametica would have died by any other cause than being hit at that very moment, at that very place?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, however, the Defence cannot accept that fact because we do not know. We have no proof what was the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you -- the position of the Defence is that she might have died -- that the death might have been caused by something else. Yes. Okay, that's clear. Then I think we dealt with most of the 92 bis issues. We will have to give decisions on that. There were other issues, Mr. Ierace, you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Timetable, Mr. President. The Rules allow the Defence, following the conclusion of the Prosecution case, seven days to file, if they wish to do so, a "no case to answer" submission. And I think the practice directions require that that be ten pages and no more. And then the Rule allows seven days to the Prosecution to reply. If the Prosecution case does conclude on the 2nd of August, one wonders, after this week's timetable, then that being the last day of term, those two weeks would, on the face of it, require both the Prosecution and the Defence to work through the break, which would be sad for both the Prosecution and the Defence, Mr. President, given that we have just finished some seven months of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you will certainly have had in mind as well what would have happened if the Prosecution would have finished its case earlier in July, what would have happened, perhaps, for the Chamber. But let's not speculate on that. Would you say that you would ask leave to reply after the recess of the Court? And I don't know whether the Defence would want to ask leave to file its motion after the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before -- might I -- it might be faster if I were to finish the submission. There is one other aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you to my learned colleague. The Rules also provide that the Defence, pursuant to Rule 65 ter (G), the Rules provide that the Trial Chamber shall order the Defence to file various documents and Rule 73 ter -- I withdraw that. And clearly implicit in that is a time limit to do so. Those documents include the names of each witness that the Defence proposes to call and a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify. There is no indication as to a time limit to do that. One assumes that that decision is made after the decision in respect of the no case to answer submissions, unless the Defence is required to contingently be ready to file those documents in case they do not succeed on the no case to answer submission. Finally, Rule 73 ter states that the Trial Chamber has the discretion as to whether it will hold a conference, that is a pre-Defence case conference. It does not have to do so, but may do so. So, Mr. President, they are the three matters which will arise predictably at the end of the Prosecution case. The reason I raise it now is this. Already I have explained the difficulties with the break in terms of the no case to answer submissions. But beyond that, the Prosecution would be grateful, and no doubt the Defence as well, for some indication, if it happens that the no case to answer submission is not successful, as to when we might expect the Defence case will commence, and more particularly, when we might expect a witness list so that the Prosecution can make necessary enquiries in relation to the witnesses; an exhibit list for the same reason. Breaking it down, Mr. President, the no case to answer submission is the most immediate issue, but beyond that, if at the time that we go on leave on the 2nd of August we had some expectations to when those other matters might arise, that will be of enormous assistance to the Prosecution in managing its resources, human and otherwise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand your concerns and what you did not say loudly is that how could you explain at home on how the holiday will be spoiled or not be spoiled. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Yes. I start from the principle that the Prosecution would sacrifice its holiday for the sake of justice and we will do the same, but I will pursue in the same direction and that is to refer to the question Mr. Ierace -- I am referring to Article 73. We shall see what we shall do. But I say that we will be answering as quickly as possible once we have detailed information and when we have all our exhibits quite clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are relating to Rule 73 -- no, I think, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are -- I did hear you say Rule 73, where you might have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 73 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it is clear to me. But are there any wishes, I mean, if you would say you first finish whenever needed within seven days a motion no case to answer, and then go on holiday, or that you would say, no, you would rather have do it after the recess or -- well, I am not saying that this would be possible. At least I would like to hear whatever wishes there would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I thought I had said so already. But clearly the Defence wishes have as much time as possible, of course, in order to prepare itself. That is obvious. Taking account of what we have heard so far, and since we are going to have the recess, the later that comes in, the better we will be prepared and, hopefully, the more satisfied the Chamber will be. At least this is our hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do understand. You want as much time as possible. Are there any other procedural issues we would have to deal with at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think we will have a break now until a quarter to -- 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the Chamber invites the Defence to file, if there is any need, submissions in relation to the 92 bis statement of Mr. Cavcic, if that could be just briefly done in writing, then we will consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the deadline for that, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two days. Would that be possible? By the end of the week. Yes? I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most likely so, as far as I am concerned, but also as far as Madam Pilipovic is concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and nodding of lead counsel is of course of major importance. Mr. Ierace, it will be Mr. Waespi who will take the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you call, the next witness will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Will be Colonel Fraser. Perhaps if the Registrar could prepare the map, the clean map, Exhibit number 3644, later to be shown to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be P3644.DF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put on the headphones of Mr. Fraser so that whenever there would be any intervention from the Defence ... Mr. Fraser, I take it that you understand me -- that you hear me in a language you understand. Before giving your testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration. And the usher has handed out the text to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for much, Mr. Fraser. Please be seated. Yes. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fraser.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state for the record your rank, name, current position?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Colonel David Fraser. I am the project director for land forces reserve restructure at army headquarters in National Defence Headquarters, Ottawa, Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever serve within the UN system in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I served from April 1994 to May 1995 at Sector Sarajevo headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to come back later in a different function?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I returned as the battle group commander as part of S4 in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fraser, may I ask you to make a small pause between the question and the answer because the interpreters need some time to translate everything both in French and Bosnian, Serbian, Croatian. So, therefore, if we go too quick, they will not cope with your speed. Please proceed. One way of doing it is looking at your screen. When the cursor stops moving, then you may answer the question. And if there is just one or two words left, you might already start.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, can we please focus on your first time in Sarajevo and also on the period between April and early August in 1994. Did you have a chance in that period to see any sniping positions in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell me with the assistance of a map, which I could kindly ask the registrar to show to the witness, where these positions were. If you, Colonel Fraser, could please indicate as good as you can, as accurate as you can, where these positions were and explain them to us. And perhaps you could use, as soon as you have identified them, for you to use a red -- I am sorry, blue pen, and indicate the area.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We looked at some positions in this area here. And in fact, I remember going with the sector commander on a tour of a number of positions, including what was referred to as the "red building." And we walked through these buildings, and we could see openings and there were boxes and sandbags where shooters could possibly set up and take a look. We looked out the windows and we could see back to the Bosniak side. We could also look down and see where some of the UN positions were, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. -- Colonel Fraser. Can you tell us who arranged those visits for you? To whom did you go to be able to see these positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We would normally do, if we wanted to go for a visit, we would get in contact with our LOs or the Fre-Bats in the area. They would arrange it through the corps headquarters or the respective brigade headquarters and we would coordinate, and we'd actually get escorted. And we were, on this occasion, we were escorted through these positions and shown around on that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what corps headquarters are you talking about, of which side of the two warring factions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was the Serbian Corps at Lukavica barracks, General Galic's headquarters at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was the person, if you could indicate his name or his rank, who had actually shown you around those sniping positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I cannot remember exact the details who actually escorted us around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know his function?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Although the booth has not protested, I think that there had been omissions of serious -- of considerable portions of the testimony, probably due to the very high speed at which the witness is speaking. We have to take into account the transcript and the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, my last question was whether you could recall the function of the person. Was he a soldier or an officer, and if he was an officer, do you recall what his function was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I knew that when we went for visits on the Serbian side, that we were always escorted by an officer. And on this particular case, it was an officer but I don't recall his name or function.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was he in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could just, for the sake of completion, add a letter "A" to the circle which you just drew out on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At that occasion or perhaps at another occasion but within the time frame between August and early -- between April and early August 1994, what kind of weaponry, sniping weaponry, have you seen, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I did not see any weaponry personally, however, the reports that we investigated included what we believed were high velocity rifles, incidents of sniping around the city, including the airport, the area I just showed you, and a place called Sedrenik or Grdonj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can take you back, Colonel Fraser, to the weaponry. Do you recall the -- you mentioned high velocity rifles. Do you recall other additions to weapons? You said you have not seen them but you said you have read reports or were given information. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We had reports and we also investigated UN positions at the Jewish cemetery that were attacked at night by grenades, rifle-launched grenades. That happened several times. Plus the shootings down along what was commonly known as "sniper alley," where we had a task force. And there were other incidents of mortaring of the city and around the area within the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion, again from personal experience or from reports you have read or seen, about the professionalism of the snipers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was our assessment that the people conducting these actions were professional because of our difficulty locating them. They were not presenting themselves in a clear view of the UN soldiers. So they were taking positions of concealment to shoot at both the civilians and UN. This indicated to us that these people knew what they were doing and were very good at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just for clarification purposes, when you describe these people, these people from part of which warring faction?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you also have an opinion, based on your information, experience, at that time, about the accuracy of sniping coming from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is my opinion, based on the reports and what I witnessed, these individuals were very good because the casualties were a direct result of their actions, and they were numerous. In talking to the soldiers, the French soldiers on -- along sniper alley, they indicated to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that we are now slowing down -- I said, not without purpose, that if there are still one or two words missing, if you take a low speed, they are always a bit behind. That is no problem. But if it becomes too much -- but then if you talk at a slow regular speed as I do it now, they will certainly be able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers indicated to us that in the morning, when they adopted their positions along sniper alley, from time to time shooters from the Serbian side would fire at a telephone pole to indicate they were in position. And once in a while they would -- I would call "range" their weapons by firing shots off the UN vehicles to get an indication of where their rifles were firing. And then they would wait during the day to conduct their operations. That indicates to me that these are people who know what they are doing and are fairly confident in their skills because there were several hundred soldiers trying to find out where these people were so that we could stop them from doing what they were there to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you tell us "that we could stop them," and I quote you, "doing what they were to do," or earlier you said and I quote you again, "to conduct their operations," what kind of operations are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In that area, there were only two or -- two groups of people: There were the UN and then there were the local Bosnian civilians. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. along that area, the sniping snipers were shooting mainly at the Bosnians, and once in a while at the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, were you able to form an opinion as to the organisation or whether there was a structure within these snipers you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is my opinion that these snipers were acting on orders from a higher organisation than the areas because the three areas that I described, Sedrenik, sniper alley and the airport, crossed a number of different Serbian brigades. And the activities appeared to have been coordinated because of the incidents and how they seemed to happen around the city, that there seemed to be some structure. And when there was an incident, we would protest. And in those protests, and in the discussions with General Galic and his headquarters, there seemed to be some control over the level of activity that these snipers had upon the citizens and the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, how many times would you talk to General Galic about this type of activity you just described?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: When I arrived in April of that year, sniping incidents had been on the rise and there had been some protests, and General Soubirou wanted to improve the situation and prevent it from getting out of control. So he asked for a meeting with General Galic sometime in May or June that year, or July, with the aim of trying to stop the killing. Because it was a tit-for-tat operation and we didn't want it to get out of control any more than it already was. So we met with him a couple of times, that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall what the response was of General Galic on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Well, General Galic would start off by lecturing us, but eventually we would discuss the incidents. And the results of these discussions, there was a notable decrease in most cases in the level of sniping activity around the city after talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you only protest because of sniping incidents or were there incidents with other weaponry which would provoke you to take protests to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We conducted protests for any sniping incident, shelling incident, weapons in the exclusion zone, if they were not in the weapon collecting points. Anytime there was a contradiction in the UN agreement, we would go to General Galic and protest those cases in two ways: We would send a letter, a written form, to him, and more effectively, we would ask for a meeting to discuss these incidents in order that we could press the point and get him to cease these activities on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the source of the information you had which enabled you to draft these letters or make these oral protests?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In the sniping incidents --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is a multiple question. It seems to concern at the same time the sniping elements and the shelling elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we turn first to sniping, what is the source of information which you had at your disposition which made you go to General Galic and make the protests you just talked about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In the case of sniping, be it rifle, grenade, or direct fire, it could be the body of a killed Bosnian, it could be the UN position that was attacked at night at Jewish cemetery, which happens several times. The results, whether they were fatal or not, were sufficient for us to make a protest because this was in contravention, that the evidence was pretty clear-cut. We had physical evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was it any different when it came to shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There was no difference when it came to shelling incidents. In that case, we would sent out a team to go find the crater, conduct a crater analysis, and then based on those results, we would go back to the applicable organisation and make the protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said that oral and written protests were made. Can you tell us whether one of them was more efficient, more effective, than the other one?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was our experience that oral protests, i.e. going to the headquarters and dealing directly with the commander, was far more effective than written protests. However, the written protest was a paper record of the actions. And in every case when we went to a meeting, we would write up those meeting notes and put them on our files.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, when you raised the issue of sniping with General Galic, what was his response, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Normally, we would receive a lecture --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am really sorry, but the question is much too general. The Prosecution has quoted 27 -- 24 incidents. They have to be addressed specifically and not all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can rephrase the question, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied so it is up to you whether you want to or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, if you could answer this question: When you went to General Galic and confronted him with a sniping incident, do you recall any specific answer he gave?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I don't recall any specific answer that he gave. I can characterise our meetings with him starting off by being lectured, a denial of what it was we were trying to discuss. However, there was some acknowledgment about sniping around the city and a general consensus that it would be nice if they had an anti-sniping agreement. One which was written up, was not signed by neither party later in that summer, but it is something that we wanted. However, having gone through the meeting with General Galic, the incidents of sniping around the city did diminish somewhat for a period of time. So the meeting was effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Turning to shelling, when you -- you said earlier that crater analysis was done at times. Did you ever take the results of any such analysis when civilians were killed to General Galic and raise it with him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I can't recall during that period of time taking those results to General Galic, no specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Earlier, you said that sniping was conducted at Bosnian civilians. Turning now to shelling, was shelling --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, from what I remember, the witness spoke about Bosnians but not about Bosnian civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just try to find the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the term used was "Bosnians." I am speaking from my memory, but I can check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the witness said Bosnian Muslims -- civilians, Bosnian civilians, in his first sentence. And in his next sentence, he only referred to Bosnians. But we can clarify that with the witness, if you wish me to do so, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, when you were earlier talking about sniping at the sniper alley, you said that UN personnel were present in that area and also Bosnian civilians. Who were the targets of sniping from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am about to check this, Mr. President. But once again, we are coming back to the same thing. One wants to say the word "Bosnian civilians," and that was the substance of my objection to this term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Either you rephrase the question, Mr. Waespi, or we find the place where the witness ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am happy to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, who were the targets of sniping from the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The targets were UN soldiers and Muslims. Bosnian Muslim citizens, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And by "citizens," do you mean military personnel or civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In the area of sniper alley, there were no military positions there. They were just civilians walking along the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Fraser. Turning to shelling, in the time again between April 1994 when you arrived in Sarajevo and early August, in your experience, from reports you have seen or personal experience, at what was the shelling directed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From my experience, shelling was directed either towards the Presidency, various parts of the city, not principally any military position. And there seemed to have been an unwritten convention that the opposing side's headquarters were not shelled. They were always left intact, but the Presidency and other parts of the city were not given the same latitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just interfere. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you would have looked at page 77, line 8, you would have read: "In that area, there were two groups of people, there were the UN and then there were the local Bosnian civilians." Please proceed, Mr. Waespi. And may I invite you next time, first to check and then to intervene. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just gave the answer, Colonel Fraser, that and I quote you: "Shelling was directed either towards the Presidency, various parts of the city, not principally any military position." What do you mean by, "not principally any military position"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In the middle of the city, there were no positions. The confrontation lines were a little bit more to the outside. So when shelling happened inside the city, when we would go and investigate or the UNMOs would go in and investigate, for the most part, there were only civilian communities or people in those areas, no military target that we could identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many times, Colonel Fraser, did you meet with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I recall a couple of times, but it has been quite some time, so I can't really remember. I know once for sure, twice probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what impression you formed about his personality and his command style, if you are able to do so?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: What I recall of General Galic was, he was a very confident man. He would take command of the situation, lecture us. He would never give us any ground or latitude. He would make sure that he argued adamantly for his position. I would not personally want to cross him because he was a very strong -- had a strong character. And negotiations with him were difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us why they were difficult?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I think it is a function that he was a very confident individual and had been doing his job for a while and he was good at what he was doing, and he was not going to allow the UN to push him around. It was his intention to try to control the UN and the situation within inside the city. And it was my commander's attempt to try to keep the situation under control and it was a -- it was difficult for both men because they were both trying to do what they had to do. And General Galic was not going to back away from the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to meet General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion about the relationship between General Mladic and General Galic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is my opinion that General Galic was a good --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President, to ask of this question about his opinion regarding this relationship, I don't know. Perhaps he could ask whether he knows what kind of a relationship they had, because I think that his opinion is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please rephrase the question in such a way that we are talking about facts? And we cannot exclude any opinions but, I would rather first see what facts we can establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: From the meetings you had with General Mladic and General Galic, do you know what relationship there was between those two Generals?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I can't answer what the direct relationship was, but they appeared to work well together. That is all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fraser. Turning to a different issue, did United Nations troops, including yourself, know where the tanks were within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes. We knew where the tanks were in the weapon collecting points, in Lukavica barracks, and there were a couple of tanks outside those positions where we knew. In fact, there was one near an apartment block in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where was that apartment block?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact area. It was in the Serbian side, somewhere between -- somewhere just west of Sedrenik. Pardon me, Skenderija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So this was a tank which was, in your assessment, under the control of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was in violation of the UN. It should have been in the weapon collecting point. However, it was our assessment that because of the location where it was, the risk to civilians did not warrant us going in to try to move or get rid of the tank. We knew where it was and we monitored it, but the collateral damage was too high for us to take direct action.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please refer to the map and draw a circle, as good as you can, as small or big as you can, around the area where you thought the tank was and mark it with a "B."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This is a guess. I am not very sure about that "B." I just remember that there was a tank somewhere in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Fraser. My last issue is the following: In those few months you were in Sarajevo, did you have a chance to talk to civilians inside the city and discuss their experience with them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We spent a lot of time moving around the city and talking to people. I had several civilian Muslims working for us, and I would ask them about what it was like to walk to and from the PTT building, what it was like to live in the city. And on our trips into the city, I would ask the locals in the shops what it was like, and a family who also lived during the time of the Second World War where the Germans had occupied their country. In all cases, they expressed the uncertainty and the terror of never knowing what was going to happen next. And you could see that they were visibly traumatized. Many people were suffering from what we would call "post-traumatic stress disorder." And the young people were particularly adversely affected, in my opinion. And the one telling statement that I have always remembered was from this one family who said that the occupation from the Germans was far more orderly and easier to deal with than this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, but it will certainly take us some time, Mr. President, because there is the translation problem. So we shall need at least two minutes to get ready -- two or three minutes, and I will see with my colleague who will be the first one. Very well. We have split our task for the reasons that you already are aware of, Mr. President. And if you will allow me, I will start the cross-examination and then Ms. Pilipovic will conclude, if you do not mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You spoke to us about snipers a moment ago and you, in answer to a Prosecutor's question, you said that their snipers came from the Serb side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please bring his microphone closer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your question is, did the snipers come from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. My question was: Is it true that you answered, and I believe your answer was, "yes."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Does it mean, Witness, that there were no snipers on the -- snipers of the Sarajevo army or on the Presidency side, as it is usually called?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There were snipers on that side, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you established that there were snipers, and who did these latter snipers fire at?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: They would fire at the Serb side, and in some cases, civilians. And with the same resolve we would protest those incidents with the Bosnian Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You tell me that these snipers on the Presidency side sought to target civilians. Is that correct? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: On the Serb side, too, but on which side the civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: On which -- the civilians on which side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In the incidents where there was sniping from the Muslim side, it would be against the Serbs, on their side of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You never heard speaking or knew that there were certain elements which sniped from the Muslim side, but targeting the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Muslims shooting Muslims, is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Exactly that, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There were stories about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you would need two minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will stop now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will stop in one or two minutes. Mr. Fraser, I would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom. The usher will escort you out of the courtroom. And would you please not speak with anyone, whoever it is, about your testimony in this court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Fraser out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am waiting for the witness to come out, and that is all. Thank you. Within the time that remains here, on page 75.9, the term "notably" was -- the term "at night" was not interpreted. Then on 77.23 I see that in French the word, "citizens" was not interpreted. On page 83 -- no, I am sorry. Generally speaking, and on a number of pages we find the term "abandonner tout de suite," which should not be used but there was again another expression which was good by the French booth. And then the last thing on 86.11, the witness said, "collateral damage was too hard" and I think he meant "us," "for us," but that UN forces -- "UNPROFOR forces" was not interpreted in French. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also gave some interpretation of what the witness meant is that the collateral damage for the UN forces was too much. That is an interpretation which is not part of translation. So, therefore, translation fine, interpretation, we will have to understand what we -- and of course, you can ask the witness during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other issues we should deal with at this moment? Then we will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.
